questions.q: Why does this lesson say the eval dataset must be built before the monitoring setup?
options: The order genuinely doesn't matter and could be done in any sequence
Monitoring must always be built first according to a strict industry standard
Everything after the eval dataset depends on knowing what 'working correctly' means for the feature — you can't meaningfully monitor for a problem you haven't defined
Eval datasets can only be written after a model card already exists
questions.explain: The lesson explains that monitoring and incident response both depend on first having a definition of correct behavior, which the eval dataset provides.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say to include 2-3 deliberately hard cases in the 15-20 case eval dataset?
options: Hard cases are required by law for any AI system
A dataset of entirely easy cases that all pass tells you nothing you didn't already believe, while hard cases actually test the system
Hard cases make the dataset take less time to build
Easy cases should be removed entirely and only hard cases should be used
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly states that an all-easy dataset confirms existing beliefs rather than genuinely testing the system, which is why hard cases matter.

questions.q: What does this lesson say 'minimum viable monitoring' for the capstone actually requires?
options: A full production-grade observability platform with real-time alerting infrastructure
Nothing at all — monitoring can be skipped for a capstone project
Logging each call's input, output, timestamp, and token count, plus one real chart of cost or latency — even a spreadsheet counts if it reflects real calls
A dedicated full-time engineering team to operate the monitoring system
questions.explain: The lesson is explicit that a production observability stack isn't required — logged real data plus one real chart is sufficient to prove visibility into the system's behavior.

questions.q: How does this lesson say the incident response plan for the capstone should be written?
options: Using generic language that could apply to any AI system in any industry
Specific to the actual feature built and its identified failure mode, covering detect, contain, communicate, and review
As a single sentence with no further detail required
Only covering the 'detect' stage and omitting the rest
questions.explain: The lesson emphasizes writing a plan specific to the student's own system and its actual most likely failure mode, not generic boilerplate.

questions.q: What does this lesson say it means if a section of the model card 'feels hard to fill in honestly'?
options: It means the student should delete that section and skip it entirely
It means the capstone has failed and must be restarted from scratch
It's useful information about the system itself, not a sign the lab is being done wrong
It means the model card format is broken and should not be used
questions.explain: The lesson reframes difficulty in honestly completing a section as a genuine finding about the system's limitations, not a mistake in the exercise.
